"You look sleazy tonight," Ma said.

"Cheap," I replied. "I'm doing cheap. Do you have any idea what it costs to achieve cheap these days? To pull off gold City of Paris three-inch platform sandals with this I. Magnin snake-print dress? I'm doing cheap."

"You look like a bird," she said, "a Halloween bird with red waxed lips."

In high school, you could either do cheap or Shakespeare—college prep or a pointy bra, ratting your hair into a bubble with a toilet brush. I wasn't permitted to do high school cheap; I wore blazers and wool skirts from the Junior League thrift shop. In high school, the rule was: don't walk between Richie, Leelee, and the baby—you might come between them. "You look like a skag with that black-eyed makeup. People are going to think you're cheap."

While I poured red food dye onto my hair to match my horse's tail for the rodeo, Ma beat her head against the wall, insisting she was only trying to make me presentable. I tried, truly I did—but the loggers, the Navy men, they always hit on me.

"Because you're an easy mark," Ma said.

And I played guilty. I played guilty every single time.

But now, I said—now I'm doing cheap.

---

Mom told me I looked trashy this evening. "Cheap"—that's the word I used. I'm going for cheap. Does she even realize what it costs nowadays to pull off cheap? These gold three-inch platform sandals from City of Paris, this snake-print I. Magnin dress? Yeah, I'm going for cheap. outputs.L3:
# On Wearing Cheap

Tonight, I am cheap on purpose. This is important to clarify, because there is a difference between accidental cheapness and the deliberate, curated version I have constructed for myself—gold platform sandals that cost more than my first month's rent, a snake-print dress that required three fittings to get the illusion of carelessness just right. The irony isn't lost on me: it takes real money to look this affordable, this disposable, this gaudy. There's a particular alchemy required to transform expensive materials into something that reads as trashy, as if the whole point of good taste is knowing exactly how to abandon it.

My mother would have had opinions about this outfit, the same opinions she had about every outfit I ever wore that wasn't buttoned up to my collarbone. She used to look at me—red lips smeared on with the confidence of someone who'd never been told they were doing it wrong, eyes rimmed in black like bruises I'd painted on myself—and call me her Halloween bird. Not a compliment. There was always an edge to it, a warning folded into the words: you look cheap, and cheap girls get treated cheap. Cheap was code for vulnerable. Cheap meant asking for it, whatever "it" was that she feared would come find me if I wasn't careful.

In high school, the world she'd built for me came with only two categories, and there was no room to maneuver between them. You were either cheap or you were Shakespeare. There was no middle ground, no acknowledgment that a girl might want to wear something trendy without it being a moral failing. So while my classmates experimented with whatever was current—platform shoes, cropped tops, the small rebellions of adolescence—I was buttoned into blazers and wool skirts, a uniform meant to signal seriousness, intelligence, untouchability. I was supposed to look like I was reading Shakespeare, not like I wanted to be looked at.

The trouble was, the uniform didn't work the way she'd hoped. My mother's attempts to make me "nice"—her word, always with that particular emphasis—were exhausting for both of us. I remember the frustration of it, literal head-banging-against-wall frustration, hers and mine both, as if she could somehow reshape my body language, my walk, my very presence into something that wouldn't attract attention. But it didn't matter what I wore. Loggers still looked. Navy guys still called out from truck windows. The wool skirt was no match for whatever it was they were seeing, or thought they were seeing, or wanted to see regardless of the fabric involved.

And I played along with the guilt, because that was the script I'd been handed. Every time a man's eyes lingered too long, every time someone said something under their breath as I passed, I felt it—that specific, gendered shame that suggests the fault must be mine, must be in the ten inches of skirt or the shade of lipstick, must be something I could have prevented if I'd just tried harder to be less visible, less present, less myself.

But tonight, the guilt isn't invited. Tonight, I am choosing the gold sandals, the snake print, the red lips—not because I've failed at looking nice, but because I've decided, finally, that cheap can be a choice rather than a verdict. I get to decide what my body means when I dress it. I get to do cheap on my own terms, deliberately, expensively, joyfully—not as an accident of circumstance or a failure of upbringing, but as a costume I'm choosing to wear, knowing exactly what it costs and exactly what it's worth.
outputs.L4:
My mother's eyes did the thing they always did when she disapproved—a quick flick from my feet to my face, cataloging every offense before her mouth even opened. I was standing in the hallway in my platform sandals, the ones with the four-inch cork soles that made me tower over her, wearing a snake-print dress that clung to my body like it had been poured on. My eyelids were smoky, my lips a deep red I'd blended myself after watching a dozen tutorials. I felt powerful. She saw something else entirely.

"You look cheap," she said, the word landing like a slap.

There was a time when that word would have sent me straight back into my closet, would have had me scrubbing my face clean and pulling on something shapeless and safe. In high school, my mother had curated my wardrobe with the precision of a stylist assembling a uniform for respectability. Pastel polos. Khaki skirts that hit exactly at the knee. Cardigans buttoned to the collarbone even in August heat. I was dressed like a catalog model for a private school that didn't exist, all pressed cotton and quiet colors, because my mother believed that a girl who dressed properly invited nothing but proper attention.

Except that wasn't true either. I remembered the boy in tenth grade who'd cornered me by the lockers, his hand grazing my waist even though I was buttoned up to my throat. I remembered telling my mother about it, expecting comfort, and instead getting an inventory of what I'd been wearing that day, as if my clothes were a confession I hadn't meant to make. "Was your shirt tucked in? Were you wearing that skirt, the shorter one?" She was already building her case before I'd finished crying. The boy's hands were never the subject. My hemline was.

It didn't matter what I wore, really. That was the thing I hadn't understood then and understood with painful clarity now. Cover myself completely and I was still catcalled walking to the bus stop. Wear a modest dress and still get looks that made my skin crawl. The clothes were never the variable. Men's entitlement was the constant, and yet somehow it was always my body, my choices, my "cheapness" that got put on trial.

So now, standing in the hallway in my snake-print dress with my mother's disapproval radiating toward me like heat off asphalt, I didn't shrink. I didn't apologize. I didn't reach for the cardigan hanging by the door the way I once might have, silently negotiating my worth down to something more palatable.

"Yeah," I said. "I know."

She blinked, thrown by my agreement where she'd expected defensiveness. "You know?"

"I picked this because it's cheap. Because cheap is fun. Because I like how it feels to wear something that doesn't ask permission." I could see her trying to find the argument in that, trying to locate the shame she expected me to feel, and finding nothing to grab onto. "I'm not dressing for anyone's approval. Not yours, not some man's, not society's idea of what a good girl wears. I'm dressing for me."

"People will get the wrong idea," she said, but her voice had lost its certainty.

"What idea is that? That I'm confident? That I like the way I look? That I'm not available for judgment?" I stepped into the platforms fully, feeling the height, feeling the ground beneath me solid despite the four inches of cork. "If someone treats me badly because of what I'm wearing, that's on them. It was always going to be on them, no matter what I had on. You just never wanted to believe that, because it's easier to control my hemline than to hold anyone else accountable."

My mother didn't have a response to that, not one she was willing to voice. She simply looked at me, the daughter she'd tried so hard to keep safe by keeping her small, unremarkable, invisible to the very forces she feared. But invisibility had never protected me. It had only taught me to apologize for existing in a body that other people had opinions about.

I picked up my bag, adjusted the strap of my dress, and walked past her toward the door. The word "cheap" followed me out into the evening air, but it didn't sting the way it used to. I'd taken it from her, turned it over in my hands, and decided it was mine now—not an accusation to survive, but a choice I got to make on my own terms.
outputs.L5:
# The City That Never Sleeps Cheap

You arrive with dreams bigger than your budget, another hopeful face stepping off the bus into a city that promises everything and gives nothing for free. The skyline glitters above you, indifferent to your empty wallet, and you wonder if you've made a terrible mistake.

But you learn quickly. You discover the cheap eats tucked behind the tourist traps—the noodle shop that costs three dollars and tastes like someone's grandmother made it with love. You find the cheap thrills that don't require a credit card: watching sunsets from rooftops you're not supposed to access, free museum days circled in red on your calendar, concerts in the park where the music costs nothing but your time.

The city teaches you that "cheap" isn't always an insult. Sometimes it's a badge of honor, a secret handshake among those who know how to survive and even thrive without much money. You start collecting these secrets like treasures: the laundromat that's always empty on Tuesday mornings, the happy hour that runs two hours longer than anywhere else, the bookstore that lets you read for hours without buying anything.

You realize the city was never asking you to be rich. It was asking you to be resourceful. And somewhere between the cheap rent in a neighborhood everyone said was "up and coming" and the free concerts in July, you stopped feeling poor and started feeling like you belonged.

The city that seemed so expensive at first reveals itself differently now—full of hidden corners where you, exactly as you are, can find your place without spending a fortune to prove you deserve to be there.

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a stream-of-consciousness narrative in first person where a young woman defends her thrift-store, sexed-up style choices against her mother's criticism, contrasting it with memories of her more "respectable" high school years.
counterfactuals.output:
The mirror's telling me something different than it told me at sixteen, and Mom's voice is doing that thing again, that thing where she doesn't even have to say anything, just stands in the doorway with her arms crossed like she's guarding a bank vault of appropriate behavior—

"You're not wearing that to your cousin's thing."

I am though. I definitely am wearing this, this dollar-fifty slip dress I found buried under a pile of Blossom-era prairie skirts at the Salvation Army on Fourth, the one with the tear near the hem that I turned into a feature instead of a flaw, safety-pinned like a Vivienne Westwood accident, and yes, it shows my bra strap, and yes, the neckline plunges somewhere past where she'd like it to stop plunging—

She's thinking about Homecoming junior year. I know she is. The pale blue dress with the cap sleeves, the one that made me look like I was going to a christening instead of a dance, the one she picked out because it was "flattering" which is Mom-code for invisible, for pre-approved, for a girl who doesn't take up space or ask questions or want anyone to look at her want—

I was so good then. Star student, church on Sundays, National Honor Society pin gleaming like a merit badge for good girl-ing, and underneath all that pressed cotton I was disappearing, actually disappearing, folding myself smaller and smaller until I was just a shape other people had decided on—

This dress cost less than her lipstick and it's mine, entirely mine, chosen by me standing in a fluorescent-lit thrift store running my hands over racks of dead women's church clothes and prom rejects until something felt like electricity, like recognition—

She doesn't get that this isn't rebellion for rebellion's sake. It's not that I'm trying to hurt her, or embarrass the family, or whatever narrative she's constructing where I'm a cautionary tale in training. It's that for the first time I'm dressing like someone who actually lives in this body instead of apologizing for it, someone who takes up space instead of shrinking to fit inside a doorway shaped like other people's comfort—

"It's not appropriate," she says, and I want to ask her: appropriate for what? For whom? Because it feels pretty appropriate for me, for this Tuesday, for this life I'm building out of secondhand silk and torn tulle and the particular confidence that comes from knowing exactly how good you look and choosing to show it anyway—

I used to think being good meant being quiet. Being seen the right amount. Now I think good means honest, means present, means not curating myself down to nothing just so nobody has to look at me and think something—

The dress stays on. I fix the safety pin. I walk past her into the hallway, into the light, into whatever version of myself I'm still figuring out how to be.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a literary short story excerpt in the style of Mary Karr or Denis Johnson, featuring a rebellious narrator recalling small-town rodeo life, loggers, and a fraught relationship with her judgmental mother.
counterfactuals.output:
The summer I turned fourteen I took up with a bull rider named Dutch Aldous who had a scar under his eye shaped like a fishhook and a way of looking at you like you were the only clear thing in a dirty window. My mother called him white trash to my face and then made him a plate of pork chops when he showed up at our door reeking of Skoal and arena dirt, because that was her particular religion—condemn a thing thoroughly, then feed it.

We lived in Chehalis then, in the wet green nowhere between two logging towns, in a house that smelled of Pine-Sol and my mother's Winstons. She worked the register at the Thriftway and came home every night with her feet swollen up like bread dough, laying into me before she even got her shoes off. You smell like cigarettes. You smell like a man's hands been on you. She had a nose for sin the way some women have a nose for rain coming, and she was rarely wrong, which made it so much worse.

The rodeo came through in July, set up in the fairgrounds behind the Grange hall, and the whole town went a little feral for three days. Loggers who'd been in the woods since March came down out of the hills smelling of two-stroke oil and pitch, their forearms scarred like river maps, and they drank at the beer garden till the sawdust turned to paste under their boots. My mother said rodeo was for people with no better way to kill themselves. She said it standing in the kitchen with a chicken thigh in her hand like a gavel.

But I loved it. God help me, I loved the chute gates banging open and the bulls coming out sideways with their hind legs kicked up toward heaven, loved the pickup men riding in fast and easy like something out of scripture, loved the announcer's voice cracking through the tinny speakers calling out hometowns—Winlock, Toledo, Packwood—like a roll call of the damned and the ordinary. I loved Dutch worst of all, the way he'd come off a bull white-faced and grinning, blood on his teeth from where he'd bit his own tongue, and find me in the stands like I was the only thing worth surviving for.

My mother watched us from the bleachers once, arms crossed over her good blouse, and afterward she said, You're going to end up just like your Aunt Ruthie, three kids and a black eye and no husband to speak of. That was her prophecy for me, delivered flat as scripture, and some nights I believed her more than I believed in God.

Dutch broke his collarbone in August riding a bull named Widowmaker, which should have told everybody something, and my mother drove me to the hospital in Centralia without a word the whole way, radio off, jaw set like she was chewing glass. She waited in the truck while I went in. When I came out two hours later she handed me a paper sack with a ham sandwich in it, still warm from sitting on the dash, and said, He's not gonna amount to anything, baby, and neither will you if you keep this up.

I ate the sandwich in silence. Outside the window the mill whistle blew for shift change, and somewhere behind us the mountains were being logged down to stubble, one tree at a time, the way my mother was always trying to whittle me down to something she could recognize. I didn't answer her. I just watched the wet road unspool ahead of us, thinking of Dutch's hand in a sling, thinking that whatever was wrong with me, it was mine, and she could stand at that particular window and stare at it all she wanted—she was never coming through the glass to get me out.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a monologue-style vignette where a woman recalls her working-class upbringing, her mother's obsession with appearances, and her own evolution from awkward teenager to someone embracing a "cheap," provocative aesthetic.
counterfactuals.output:
My mother ironed everything—dish towels, my father's undershirts, even the receiving blankets before I was born, like the crease itself could confer some kind of dignity we couldn't otherwise afford. We lived in a duplex on Maple that smelled like fryer grease from the Chinese place downstairs, and she kept a lipstick—just one, Fire and Ice, Revlon, the good kind—in her purse at all times, rationed like medicine. She'd put it on before the grocery store. Before the parent-teacher conference where Mrs. Halloran looked at our shoes and decided everything she needed to know about us. My mother believed appearances were armor. She believed if you looked poor, people treated you poor, and she was probably right, but I didn't understand yet that the armor could also be a cage.

I was an ugly teenager—not tragically, just unfinished, all elbows and a nose I hadn't grown into, hair that frizzed if you looked at it wrong. I wore my cousin's hand-me-downs a size too big because my mother thought bigger meant modest meant respectable, and I remember standing in the school bathroom just staring at myself, trying to figure out what expression might make me disappear a little. I wanted so badly to be the kind of girl who didn't try, who was effortless, because effortless was expensive and I understood even then that we didn't have that particular currency.

Somewhere in my twenties, broke and reckless in a way that felt like freedom because for once nobody was watching to correct me, I found the drugstore aisle and fell in love with it—the frosted blues, the glitter that wouldn't stay put, lip liner two shades darker than the lipstick because that's what the girls at the gas station wore and they looked like they knew something I didn't. I started buying gold-plated hoops from the flea market, the kind that turn your earlobes green by June, and I wore them anyway, wore them proudly, because there was something in the cheapness itself that felt like telling the truth. My mother's whole life had been a performance of having enough. Mine became a performance of not caring that I didn't.

People call it trashy. I call it inheritance, worn inside out. Every drugstore eyeshadow, every acrylic nail chipped by Tuesday, every syllable of gum-snapping vowel my mother spent thirty years trying to iron out of my voice—I kept it. Not because I don't know better. Because I finally understand that "better" was never really about beauty. It was about her fear, dressed up and standing very straight, and I got tired of wearing her fear like it was mine.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
